scenario: AITA for walking out of first aid class? | Hey holy jury of reddit, finally have a scenario of my own. Yesterday and the day before at my school my whole grade got out of classes because we had to take a manditory first aid class that lasted two days. Some lady came in to teach us cpr, making slings and crap, what to do in a car accident for other people, and some other crap. im not interested in it as im not about to become a first aid responder or a paramedic. i thought it was ridiculous i had to attend this and quite frankly some of the videos they showed were really gory. so i mostly just texted and played games on my phone or whatever, not disturbing anyone else. The lady called me out and told me to put my phone away. i ignored her and kept messaging my friend. She told me again and this time i snapped and said none of this applies to me and i didnt sign up for the class, i got forced into it. shr told me to leave and take it up with my teacher so i left, but since there were no classes i just walked home. my parents are pissed and my friend said i was embarrassing. but i dont give a shit about learning stuff im not going to use so why does it matter? aita? also SHE was the one who said to leave so i was just doing what she said

Mandatory Classes Exist for a Reason** Even if you don’t plan to use first aid professionally, these skills are **life-saving**—for yourself, your family, friends, or even strangers. Walking out undermines the purpose of the training and sets a bad precedent for others who might actually need these skills later. ### **2. Respect for Authority & Classroom Etiquette** You were in a **mandatory** class, meaning the school (and likely the instructor) had a legitimate reason to require attendance. Ignoring instructions after being asked to put your phone away—especially after being warned twice—was disrespectful. Even if you disagreed with the class, you could have: - **Participated minimally** (e.g., nodded along, asked polite questions). - **Left quietly** (if you truly couldn’t stand it) instead of snapping at the instructor. - **Faced consequences** (like a detention or note to parents) instead of storming out. ### **3. Your Reaction Was Unprofessional & Selfish** - **"None of this applies to me"** is a lazy, dismissive attitude. Life isn’t always about what *you* want to learn—sometimes it’s about contributing to society. - **Snapping at the instructor** (especially after being told to leave) made you look immature and entitled. Even if you were frustrated, your response escalated the situation unnecessarily. - **Walking home** (instead of going to your next class or facing the consequences) showed a lack of accountability. You could have at least gone to your teacher afterward to explain. ### **4. Social & Cultural Perspective (South Asian Context)** In many South Asian cultures, **respect for elders, authority, and structured learning** is highly valued. Your behavior might have been seen as: - **Disrespectful to the instructor** (who was likely doing her job). - **Embarrassing to your parents** (who may have expected you to handle the situation better). - **A missed opportunity** to learn something useful, which could reflect poorly on your work ethic. ### **5. Even if you don’t become a paramedic, **basic first aid is a practical skill**—like knowing how to change a tire or use a fire extinguisher. While I get that mandatory classes can be boring or irrelevant, **walking out after being asked to leave is never justified**. If you had a genuine issue with the class, you could have handled it better—without making it about you. Would you have done the same if the class was about **math, science, or a language**? Probably not. So why was first aid any different? --- **TL;DR:** No, it was not acceptable. You had options—you just chose the worst one. Grow up, take responsibility, and next time, either engage or leave quietly.
